patient.chief_complaint: Confusion and agitation after brief seizure, not returning to normal after 40 minutes, fever noted by EMS
patient.history_present_illness: A 34-year-old White female graphic designer was brought by EMS to the emergency department after her roommate found her having a brief generalized seizure lasting 2 minutes and called 911. The roommate reports the patient had been unwell for 5 days with progressively worsening headache, confusion, and behavioral changes — she was talking to herself, becoming paranoid, and at one point undressing in the living room. She had reduced oral intake for 3 days. The roommate noted the patient had no history of seizures. On EMS arrival, the patient was minimally responsive, combative, with a temperature of 38.9°C measured by EMS. In the ED she is markedly agitated, requiring soft restraints, not following commands, with disorganized speech, and responding to internal stimuli (appears to be hallucinating). The patient wore a medic alert bracelet that says 'no known allergies.' Comprehensive urine drug screen is negative.

Protein 68 mg/dL (elevated; reference 15-45). Glucose 52 mg/dL (serum 96; ratio 0.54). Anti-NMDAR IgG CSF: POSITIVE at 1:32 titer. HSV-1/2, VZV, EBV, CMV PCRs: all negative. output.query: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis treatment immunotherapy teratoma outcome

results.finding: In cohort studies, approximately 80% of patients with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis show full or near-full recovery; immunotherapy and, when applicable, tumor removal are associated with better outcomes.
Second-line immunotherapy agents (rituximab, cyclophosphamide) have been used in cases not responding to first-line treatment; functional recovery may require weeks to months.

In patients with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis associated with ovarian teratoma, surgical removal of the tumor has been associated with improved neurological outcomes and reduced relapse risk in observational series.

Seizures and non-convulsive status epilepticus are reported in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis; the extreme delta brush EEG pattern has been described in this condition, with reported specificity over 90% in some series.

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Lymphocytic pleocytosis with oligoclonal bands; CSF NMDAR IgG positive (definitive)

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Right ovarian teratoma identified — needs surgical removal as definitive immunomodulation

optimal_actions.action: Draw two sets of blood cultures, aerobic and anaerobic, before the first antimicrobial dose
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Growth identifies the organism and its susceptibility; a negative or pending culture does not exclude the diagnosis, and yield falls once treatment has started

useless_tools.rationale: Autonomic instability is monitored at the bedside in ICU; ambulatory Holter not indicated acutely.
Neuropsychological battery cannot be performed in encephalopathic patient and does not change acute management.

sequence_constraints.reason: CT before LP to exclude mass effect (especially with focal seizure features).
Confirm beta-hCG before any imaging with contrast and before AED selection.

critical_actions: Administer IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg first-line; do not delay for diagnostics
Start empiric IV acyclovir until HSV PCR returns
Load levetiracetam as ESETT second-line (avoid valproate in reproductive-age women)
Initiate first-line immunotherapy (high-dose methylprednisolone + IVIG) once NMDAR encephalitis is the working diagnosis
Pelvic imaging and gynecology consult for teratoma removal — definitive treatment
Avoid haloperidol / first-gen antipsychotics in suspected anti-NMDAR
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT administer haloperidol / first-gen antipsychotics for agitation — risk of severe dystonia/NMS in NMDAR encephalitis
Do NOT defer LP once CT excludes mass effect — CSF NMDAR antibody is definitive
Do NOT delay teratoma removal once identified — tumor is the immunogenic source

Do NOT use haloperidol or first-generation antipsychotics for agitation in suspected anti-NMDAR encephalitis — risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome / severe dystonia; avoid until diagnosis excluded.
key_reasoning_points: Young woman with new-onset seizures + psychiatric features + autonomic instability + fever = consider anti-NMDAR encephalitis until proven otherwise
CSF NMDAR antibody is more sensitive than serum; both should be sent
Ovarian teratoma is found in ~50% of female anti-NMDAR patients; removal is the most important treatment
MRI is normal in ~50% of anti-NMDAR — a normal MRI does not exclude the diagnosis

red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests bacterial / viral CNS infection as primary cause, prompting protracted infectious workup before autoimmune testing
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Anti-NMDAR encephalitis commonly produces fever and inflammatory markers; CSF NMDAR antibody and pelvic imaging for teratoma are required to nail the diagnosis
